course.title: Introduction to Programming in Python
course.summary: Writing small Python scripts: data, control flow, functions, collections, errors, modules and files.
course.note: Objective wording is Recall Lab's own paraphrase of the publicly described course competencies; it is not official WGU or zyBooks material.

competencies.title: Scripts with control flow
competencies.summary: Write Python programs that store data, make decisions, repeat work, organise logic into functions and handle errors.

competencies.title: Reuse and file I/O
competencies.summary: Pull in functionality from modules and the standard library, and read and write files.

objectives.title: Variables, expressions & operators
objectives.summary: Assign and update variables; evaluate arithmetic with + - * / // % ** and precedence; use augmented assignment.

objectives.title: Input, output & type conversion
objectives.summary: Read text with input(), convert with int(), float() and str(), and format output with print options and f-strings.

objectives.title: Branching & Boolean logic
objectives.summary: Write if / elif / else chains; combine conditions with and, or, not; reason about comparisons and truthiness.

objectives.title: Loops
objectives.summary: Repeat work with for over range() and sequences, and with while; use break, continue, accumulators and nested loops.

objectives.title: Functions
objectives.summary: Define functions with parameters, defaults and return values; tell return from print; understand local vs global scope.

objectives.title: Strings
objectives.summary: Index and slice strings, use common string methods, and remember that strings are immutable.

objectives.title: Lists & tuples
objectives.summary: Create, index, slice and change lists; use list methods and comprehensions; know when to use an immutable tuple.

objectives.title: Dictionaries & sets
objectives.summary: Store and look up key-value pairs, iterate with items(), use get() and membership tests, and de-duplicate with sets.

objectives.title: Exceptions & debugging
objectives.summary: Read tracebacks, recognise common runtime errors, and handle them with try / except / else / finally and raise.

objectives.title: Modules & libraries
objectives.summary: Import modules in different ways and use standard-library modules such as math, random, datetime and string; know what __name__ == '__main__' does.

objectives.title: Files
objectives.summary: Open files in the right mode, read and write text, close files automatically with with, and process CSV-style rows.

questions.prompt: Which operator gives the remainder after integer division?
questions.explanation:
**What the question is asking**

Which operator gives the remainder after integer division?

**The answer**

The right choice is `%`.

**The idea, step by step**

A variable is a name stuck on a value, like a label on a box. `=` stores a value in that name. Python does math in a fixed order: parentheses first, then `**` (to the power of), then `*`, `/`, `//` and `%` from left to right, then `+` and `-` from left to right. `//` keeps only how many whole times one number fits in another. `%` is the leftover. `/` always keeps a decimal.

Division of whole numbers asks two different questions. How many times does the second number fit? What is left over?

The leftover is called the remainder. The symbol for it is `%`. Picture 17 cookies and 5 people. Each person gets 3 (that uses 15). 2 cookies remain, so `17 % 5` is 2.

`//` answers "how many whole times?" and would give 3. `/` keeps the decimal, so 17 / 5 is 3.4. `**` means "to the power of". Only `%` is the remainder.

The one-line version: `%` (modulo) returns the remainder: 17 % 5 is 2. `//` is floor division (the whole-number quotient), `/` is true division and always gives a float, and `**` is exponentiation.

**Keep this**

If another choice looks familiar, read the steps once more before you move on. The choice that fits is `%`.

questions.prompt: What is the value of `7 / 2` in Python 3?
questions.explanation:
**What the question is asking**

What is the value of `7 / 2` in Python 3?

**The answer**

The right choice is `3.5`.

**The idea, step by step**

A variable is a name stuck on a value, like a label on a box. `=` stores a value in that name. Python does math in a fixed order: parentheses first, then `**` (to the power of), then `*`, `/`, `//` and `%` from left to right, then `+` and `-` from left to right. `//` keeps only how many whole times one number fits in another. `%` is the leftover. `/` always keeps a decimal.

In Python 3, the single slash `/` means "divide and keep the fraction". 7 divided by 2 is three and a half, written `3.5`. The result is a float, which is a number that can have a decimal point.

It is not the whole number 3. That would be floor division, written `//`. It is not 3.0 either: 3.0 would mean the math came out even, and 7 / 2 does not. It is not rounded up to 4.

So `7 / 2` is `3.5`.

The one-line version: In Python 3 the `/` operator always performs true division and returns a float, so 7 / 2 is 3.5. Use `//` if you want the floor quotient 3.

**Keep this**

If another choice looks familiar, read the steps once more before you move on. The choice that fits is `3.5`.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a valid variable name?
questions.explanation:
**What the question is asking**

Which of these is a valid variable name?

**The answer**

The right choice is `total_cost`.

**The idea, step by step**

A variable is a name stuck on a value, like a label on a box. `=` stores a value in that name. Python does math in a fixed order: parentheses first, then `**` (to the power of), then `*`, `/`, `//` and `%` from left to right, then `+` and `-` from left to right. `//` keeps only how many whole times one number fits in another. `%` is the leftover. `/` always keeps a decimal.

A variable name is a label you invent. It may use letters, digits, and the underscore `_`. It cannot start with a digit, so `2nd_place` is illegal.

A hyphen is the minus sign. Python reads `total-cost` as "total minus cost", not as one name. `class` is already a Python word, so you cannot use it as a label.

`total_cost` follows the rules: letters and one underscore, and it does not start with a digit.

The one-line version: Names may contain letters, digits and underscores but cannot start with a digit. A hyphen is read as minus, and `class` is a reserved keyword.

**Keep this**

If another choice looks familiar, read the steps once more before you move on. The choice that fits is `total_cost`.

questions.prompt: What is the value of `2 + 3 * 4 ** 2`?
questions.explanation:
**What the question is asking**

What is the value of `2 + 3 * 4 ** 2`?

**The answer**

The right choice is `50`.

**The idea, step by step**

A variable is a name stuck on a value, like a label on a box. `=` stores a value in that name. Python does math in a fixed order: parentheses first, then `**` (to the power of), then `*`, `/`, `//` and `%` from left to right, then `+` and `-` from left to right. `//` keeps only how many whole times one number fits in another. `%` is the leftover. `/` always keeps a decimal.

Python does not simply go left to right. Powers happen first, then multiplication, then addition.

`4 ** 2` is 4 times 4, which is 16. Then `3 * 16` is 48. Then `2 + 48` is 50.

400 would mean someone did `(2 + 3 * 4) ** 2` or grouped differently. 80 and 196 are other grouping mistakes. The value is 50.

The one-line version: Exponentiation binds tightest (4 ** 2 = 16), then multiplication (3 * 16 = 48), then addition (2 + 48 = 50).

**Keep this**

If another choice looks familiar, read the steps once more before you move on. The choice that fits is `50`.

questions.prompt: What does `-7 // 2` evaluate to?
questions.explanation:
**What the question is asking**

What does `-7 // 2` evaluate to?

**The answer**

The right choice is `-4`.

**The idea, step by step**

A variable is a name stuck on a value, like a label on a box. `=` stores a value in that name. Python does math in a fixed order: parentheses first, then `**` (to the power of), then `*`, `/`, `//` and `%` from left to right, then `+` and `-` from left to right. `//` keeps only how many whole times one number fits in another. `%` is the leftover. `/` always keeps a decimal.

Floor division `//` does not chop toward zero. It moves toward negative infinity, which means "down" on the number line, even for negative numbers.

`-7 / 2` is -3.5. The next whole number down from -3.5 is -4, not -3. -3 would be closer to zero. -3.5 is the exact division, which `/` would give, not `//`.

So `-7 // 2` is -4.

The one-line version: Floor division rounds toward negative infinity, not toward zero. -3.5 floors to -4.

**Keep this**

If another choice looks familiar, read the steps once more before you move on. The choice that fits is `-4`.

questions.prompt: After `x = 10` then `x -= 3` then `x *= 2`, what is x?
questions.explanation:
**What the question is asking**

After `x = 10` then `x -= 3` then `x *= 2`, what is x?

**The answer**

The right choice is `14`.

**The idea, step by step**

A variable is a name stuck on a value, like a label on a box. `=` stores a value in that name. Python does math in a fixed order: parentheses first, then `**` (to the power of), then `*`, `/`, `//` and `%` from left to right, then `+` and `-` from left to right. `//` keeps only how many whole times one number fits in another. `%` is the leftover. `/` always keeps a decimal.

`x -= 3` means `x = x - 3`. `x *= 2` means `x = x * 2`. Each line uses the value x has at that moment.

Start at 10. Subtract 3 and x is 7. Multiply by 2 and x is 14.

17 would be 10 + 3 + something else. 4 would be if you subtracted after multiplying. 20 would be if you only multiplied. The stored value is 14.

The one-line version: Augmented assignment updates in place: 10 - 3 = 7, then 7 * 2 = 14.

**Keep this**

If another choice looks familiar, read the steps once more before you move on. The choice that fits is `14`.

**What the question is asking**

What is `2 ** 3 ** 2`?

**The answer**

The right choice is `512`.

**The idea, step by step**

A variable is a name stuck on a value, like a label on a box. `=` stores a value in that name. Python does math in a fixed order: parentheses first, then `**` (to the power of), then `*`, `/`, `//` and `%` from left to right, then `+` and `-` from left to right. `//` keeps only how many whole times one number fits in another. `%` is the leftover. `/` always keeps a decimal.

When two `**` operators sit in a row, Python does the right-hand one first. It does not go left to right.

So `2 ** 3 ** 2` means `2 ** (3 ** 2)`. `3 ** 2` is 9. `2 ** 9` is 512.

questions.prompt: Which statement swaps the values of `a` and `b` in one line?
questions.explanation:
**What the question is asking**

Which statement swaps the values of `a` and `b` in one line?

**The answer**

The right choice is `a, b = b, a`.

**The idea, step by step**

A variable is a name stuck on a value, like a label on a box. `=` stores a value in that name. Python does math in a fixed order: parentheses first, then `**` (to the power of), then `*`, `/`, `//` and `%` from left to right, then `+` and `-` from left to right. `//` keeps only how many whole times one number fits in another. `%` is the leftover. `/` always keeps a decimal.

`a, b = b, a` swaps two names in one line. Python first notes both values on the right, then stores them on the left. Nothing is lost.

`a = b` followed by `b = a` does not swap. After the first line both names hold the old b, so the original a is gone. `a == b` only asks whether they are equal. It stores nothing. There is no built-in `swap` function.

The one-line swap is `a, b = b, a`.

The one-line version: Tuple packing/unpacking evaluates the right side first, then assigns, so `a, b = b, a` swaps. `a = b; b = a` loses the original value of a.

**Keep this**

If another choice looks familiar, read the steps once more before you move on. The choice that fits is `a, b = b, a`.

questions.prompt: What is `round(2.5)` in Python 3?
questions.explanation:
**What the question is asking**

What is `round(2.5)` in Python 3?

**The answer**

The right choice is `2`.

**The idea, step by step**

A variable is a name stuck on a value, like a label on a box. `=` stores a value in that name. Python does math in a fixed order: parentheses first, then `**` (to the power of), then `*`, `/`, `//` and `%` from left to right, then `+` and `-` from left to right. `//` keeps only how many whole times one number fits in another. `%` is the leftover. `/` always keeps a decimal.

`round` usually moves to the nearest whole number. The awkward case is exactly halfway, like 2.5.

Python 3 uses banker's rounding: a halfway number goes to the nearest even whole number. 2 is even, 3 is odd, so 2.5 goes to 2. (3.5 would go to 4, because 4 is the even neighbor.)

It does not stay 2.5, and it does not become 2.0 unless you asked for a float. `round(2.5)` is 2.

The one-line version: Python 3 uses banker's rounding (round half to even), so 2.5 rounds to 2 while 3.5 rounds to 4.

**Keep this**

If another choice looks familiar, read the steps once more before you move on. The choice that fits is `2`.

**The answer**

**The idea, step by step**

A condition is a yes-or-no question. `if` runs its indented lines only when the answer is yes. `elif` is another question, asked only if the earlier ones were no. `else` is the backup when every question was no. Only one branch runs. `==` asks "are these equal?" A single `=` stores a value. It does not compare.

A function is a named recipe. `def` creates it and does not run it yet. The names in parentheses are parameters, slots for the values you pass in. `return` hands a value back to the caller. `print` only shows text. If there is no `return`, the function hands back `None`, which means nothing.

A function is a named recipe you can run later. Python starts that recipe with the keyword `def`, then the name, then parentheses, then a colon. The steps of the recipe are indented underneath.

`function`, `fun`, and `define` are not Python keywords.

You define a function with `def`.

`return` is how a function hands a value back. If the function never reaches a `return`, Python still has to hand something back. That something is `None`, which means "no value".

Which mode opens a file for reading?

**The answer**

The right choice is `'r'`.

**The idea, step by step**

Open a file before you read or write it. `'r'` reads. `'w'` starts the file over and erases what was there. `'a'` adds to the end. `with open(...) as f` closes the file for you even if something goes wrong. `write` does not add a new line unless you include `\n` yourself.

The mode is a short letter that says what you intend to do with a file. `'r'` means read. It is also the default if you leave the mode off. The file must already exist.

`'w'` writes and erases what was there. `'a'` appends, adding to the end. `'x'` creates a new file and fails if the file already exists.

The reading mode is `'r'`.

The one-line version: 'r' (the default) reads. 'w' truncates/creates for writing, 'a' appends, 'x' creates and fails if the file exists.

Mode `'w'` means "write, starting over". If the file already exists, its old contents are erased as soon as you open it. Then you write the new text.

`with open(...) as f` is a context manager. It opens the file, runs the indented block, and then closes the file for you. The close happens even if the block raises an error. You do not have to remember `f.close()`.

It is not a speed trick, and it is not only for writing. It does not lock the file forever. Closing is the point.

The file is closed automatically when the block ends, even after an error.
